title: OpenAI Just Hired Uber's India Boss to Run Its Second-Largest Market
excerpt: Prabhjeet Singh, who spent a decade building Uber across India and South Asia, will take over as OpenAI's first managing director for India in September — a market with 100 million weekly ChatGPT users.
body:
OpenAI has appointed Prabhjeet Singh, the outgoing president of Uber India and South Asia, as its first managing director for India, signalling that the maker of ChatGPT is no longer content with treating the subcontinent as a user base to be served remotely. It wants someone on the ground, with a local rolodex, building a real business.

Singh will join in September and report to Kiran Mani, OpenAI's managing director for Asia Pacific. He will be the company's most senior executive in India, overseeing consumer growth, enterprise adoption, strategic partnerships, regulatory engagement and day-to-day operations.

## Why India, Why Now

The arithmetic is straightforward. India is OpenAI's second-largest market after the United States, with more than 100 million weekly active ChatGPT users. That user base has been growing organically — driven by students, developers, freelance professionals and a rising wave of enterprise experimentation — but OpenAI has had limited on-the-ground leadership to convert that attention into revenue.

The company opened its first office in New Delhi in November 2025, and plans to expand to Mumbai and Bengaluru during 2026. Until now, however, it has operated in India without a country-level managing director — an unusual gap for a market of this size.



> **"Amazon announced a $48 billion India investment plan through 2030, with $21 billion earmarked for AI and cloud infrastructure."**


Singh's appointment fills that gap with a profile that maps directly onto OpenAI's challenges. At Uber, he spent nearly 11 years building a consumer technology business in one of the world's most fragmented and regulation-heavy markets. He expanded Uber beyond ride-hailing into Auto, Moto and Shuttle services, pursued electric mobility initiatives, and navigated India's Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) — the government's ambitious effort to build a public alternative to proprietary commerce platforms.

## The IIT-IIM Pipeline Continues

Singh's background — IIT Kharagpur, IIM Ahmedabad, McKinsey, Lehman Brothers, then a decade at Uber — is a familiar arc in the Indian tech diaspora. What is notable is the direction of travel: he is moving from running a large multinational's India operations into the same role at the company that arguably sits at the centre of the AI revolution.

Before Uber, he was an associate partner at McKinsey and earlier worked on the structured finance and equities trading desks at Lehman Brothers in London. That combination of consulting, finance and operational experience in India is exactly the profile that global AI companies need as they move from developer evangelism to enterprise sales and government partnerships.

## The Competitive Landscape

OpenAI is not making this move in isolation. The past month has seen an extraordinary pile-up of AI investment commitments in India. Amazon announced a $48 billion India investment plan through 2030, with $21 billion earmarked for AI and cloud infrastructure. Microsoft had already committed $17.5 billion, and Google has pledged $15 billion for data centre expansion in southern India. Add them together and Big Tech has committed more than $80 billion to India's AI infrastructure.

For OpenAI, the challenge is different from the hyperscalers. Amazon, Microsoft and Google are building the compute layer — data centres, chips, cloud services. OpenAI needs to build the application and enterprise layer on top of that infrastructure. Singh's job will be to persuade Indian enterprises, government agencies and developers that ChatGPT and OpenAI's API products are worth paying for, rather than defaulting to free tiers or open-source alternatives from Meta and China's DeepSeek.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

The appointment is one more data point in a pattern that has been accelerating: senior Indian-origin tech leaders are increasingly gravitating toward AI-native companies. Sriram Krishnan just left his role as White House AI adviser at the end of June. Sundar Pichai and Satya Nadella continue to lead Google and Microsoft as both companies bet their futures on AI. And now Singh moves from Uber to OpenAI.

For Indian engineers and product managers in the US and UK watching this space, the signal is clear — AI leadership roles in India are multiplying, and the career path between Silicon Valley and Indian AI is becoming a two-way street. For NRI investors, OpenAI's growing India bet reinforces a broader thesis: the country is moving from being a source of AI talent to becoming a primary market for AI products and services.
